Passage I


The Conference of the Parties (COP) to the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC)
constitutes the supreme decision-making body of the Convention and meets annually to assess progress in dealing
with climate change. Established at the Rio Earth Summit in 1992, the UNFCCC entered into force in 1994 and
today has near-universal membership. Each edition of the COP is hosted by a different nation on a rotating regional
basis, entailing considerable diplomatic, logistical, and financial obligations on the host country.
India has been an active participant in global climate negotiations, having submitted its updated Nationally
Determined Contributions (NDCs) to the UNFCCC in 2022 in line with its obligations under the Paris Agreement.
India's climate targets span emissions intensity reduction, renewable energy capacity, and carbon-sink creation.
Recently, credible reports have emerged indicating that India has expressed reluctance to take on the hosting of
COP33, which had been earmarked for 2028. The development has reignited international debate about equitable
burden-sharing in global climate diplomacy and the financial demands that COP hosting places on developing
economies.


Q1. The Paris Agreement, adopted at COP21 in Paris in 2015, is described as legally binding. Which of the
following most accurately characterises its legal architecture?
    a) The Paris Agreement imposes legally binding absolute emission reduction targets on all signatory states.
    b) The Paris Agreement is a binding framework under the UNFCCC, but the Nationally Determined
    Contributions (NDCs) submitted by individual parties are nationally determined and not legally binding in their
    content.
    c) The Paris Agreement is a soft-law instrument with no legally binding obligations whatsoever.
    d) The Paris Agreement is legally binding only on Annex I (developed) countries, exempting developing nations
    entirely.


Q2. COP1, the first Conference of the Parties to the UNFCCC, was held in Berlin in 1995 and resulted in the Berlin
Mandate. What was the principal significance of the Berlin Mandate?
   a) It adopted the Kyoto Protocol, setting the first binding emission reduction targets for developed nations.
   b) It recognised that existing UNFCCC commitments were inadequate and mandated negotiations for a protocol
   committing developed countries to binding emission reduction targets for the first commitment period — a
   process that culminated in the Kyoto Protocol in 1997.
   c) It established the Green Climate Fund to assist developing countries in meeting their climate obligations.
   d) It formally brought the UNFCCC into force and admitted China and India as Annex II parties.


Q3. India's reported reluctance to host COP33 in 2028 comes at a time when COP30 — the most consequential
stocktake edition since Paris — is scheduled for 2025. In which city and country is COP30 to be held?
    a) Nairobi, Kenya
    b) Belem, Brazil
    c) Dubai, UAE
    d) Sydney, Australia

Q4. India submitted its updated NDCs to the UNFCCC in August 2022. Which of the following is NOT among
India's officially stated NDC targets for 2030?
    a) Reduce the emissions intensity of GDP by 45% compared to 2005 levels by 2030.
    b) Achieve about 50% cumulative electric power installed capacity from non-fossil fuel-based energy resources
    by 2030.
    c) Create an additional carbon sink of 2.5 to 3 billion tonnes of CO2 equivalent through forest and tree cover
    by 2030.
    d) Achieve net-zero carbon emissions by 2047, coinciding with the centenary of Independence.


Q5. COP28, held in Dubai, UAE in 2023, is widely regarded as a watershed edition. Which of the following
outcomes of COP28 was described as a historic first in the history of climate negotiations?
    a) Adoption of the Loss and Damage fund as a new climate finance mechanism.
    b) Completion of the first Global Stocktake under the Paris Agreement and the adoption of language calling on
    nations to transition away from fossil fuels.
    c) Entry into force of the Kyoto Protocol's second commitment period.
    d) Agreement to limit global warming to 1.0°C above pre-industrial levels.


Q6. A fund dedicated to addressing 'loss and damage' — economic and non-economic harm caused to vulnerable
nations by climate change impacts they cannot adapt to — was established by agreement at COP27 in Sharm el-
Sheikh. At which subsequent COP was this fund formally operationalised, with its Board constituted and initial
pledges received?
    a) COP26, Glasgow
    b) COP27, Sharm el-Sheikh itself
    c) COP28, Dubai
    d) COP29, Baku



Passage II


The Constitution of India provides for the independence of the judiciary through a carefully circumscribed removal
process for judges of the Supreme Court and High Courts. Articles 124(4) and 218, read with the Judges (Inquiry)
Act, 1968, prescribe that a judge may be removed by the President only after an address by each House of Parliament
supported by a majority of the total membership of that House as well as by a majority of not less than two-thirds
of members of that House present and voting. This onerous threshold reflects the constitutional commitment to
judicial independence.
In an unprecedented controversy, Justice Yashwant Varma, a serving judge, came under intense scrutiny following
a reported discovery of a large quantity of unaccounted cash at his official residence in New Delhi, an incident that
came to light during a fire at the premises. The Supreme Court constituted an in-house inquiry committee to examine
the matter. Following the committee's proceedings and the Chief Justice of India's communication to the executive,
Justice Varma tendered his resignation, effectively ending the formal parliamentary impeachment process before it
could be initiated. The episode has reignited debate on judicial accountability mechanisms in India.

Q7. In the annals of judicial impeachment in India, which judge holds the distinction of being the first against
whom the Rajya Sabha passed an impeachment motion, only for the process to terminate when the judge resigned
before the Lok Sabha could vote on the motion?
    a) Justice V. Ramaswami of the Supreme Court of India
    b) Justice P.D. Dinakaran of the Karnataka High Court
    c) Justice Soumitra Sen of the Calcutta High Court
    d) Justice C.S. Karnan of the Madras High Court


Q8. Under the Judges (Inquiry) Act, 1968, when a motion for removal of a Supreme Court judge has been admitted,
a three-member investigation committee is constituted. Which of the following correctly states the composition of
this committee?
     a) The Chief Justice of India, the Attorney General of India, and one distinguished jurist nominated by the
     Speaker/Chairman.
     b) The Chief Justice of India or a Judge of the Supreme Court nominated by the Chief Justice, a Chief Justice
     of a High Court nominated by the Chief Justice of India, and a distinguished jurist nominated by the Speaker
     or the Chairman.
     c) Three sitting Judges of the Supreme Court nominated by the Chief Justice of India.
     d) The Chief Justice of India, the Solicitor General of India, and the Comptroller and Auditor General of India.


Q9. The controversy involving Justice Yashwant Varma came to public attention because of what specific triggering
event at his official New Delhi residence?
    a) A CBI search operation conducted pursuant to a Supreme Court order
    b) An Income Tax Department survey authorised by the Finance Ministry
    c) A fire at his official residence, during the response to which large quantities of cash were allegedly discovered
    by firefighting personnel
    d) A whistleblower complaint filed by a member of the Supreme Court Bar Association


Q10. At the time of the cash-discovery controversy, Justice Yashwant Varma was serving as a judge of which High
Court?
   a) Allahabad High Court
   b) Delhi High Court
   c) Bombay High Court
   d) Madhya Pradesh High Court


Q11. The constitutional threshold for passing a removal motion against a Supreme Court judge in each House of
Parliament is deliberately stringent. Which of the following correctly states this threshold?
    a) A simple majority of members present and voting in both Houses.
    b) A two-thirds majority of the total membership of each House.
    c) A majority of the total membership of the House AND not less than two-thirds of the members of that House
    present and voting — both conditions must be satisfied simultaneously.
    d) A three-fourths majority of members present and voting in the Rajya Sabha, and a simple majority in the Lok
    Sabha.

Q12. Under the Supreme Court's in-house procedure for dealing with allegations of misconduct against a sitting
judge, if an inquiry committee finds the allegations to be proved and the judge declines to resign, what is the
prescribed next step?
    a) The Chief Justice of India may directly order the removal of the judge by administrative resolution.
    b) The President of India may act suo motu to remove the judge upon the recommendation of the Chief Justice.
    c) The Chief Justice of India transmits the inquiry committee's report to the Speaker of the Lok Sabha and the
    Chairman of the Rajya Sabha, enabling them to initiate the formal parliamentary address process under Article
    124(4).
    d) The collegium convenes a special sitting to suspend the judge from judicial functions pending parliamentary
    action.



Passage III


Great Nicobar Island, the southernmost and largest island of the Nicobar archipelago, is a Union Territory of India.
Situated at the confluence of the Indian Ocean and the Andaman Sea, it occupies a position of significant strategic
salience given its proximity to one of the world's busiest maritime chokepoints. The island is home to the Shompen,
a particularly vulnerable hunter-gatherer tribal group recognised as a Particularly Vulnerable Tribal Group (PVTG),
and the Nicobarese, both of whom hold special constitutional and statutory protections.
The Government of India, through NITI Aayog, has proposed a Holistic Development Plan for the island that
envisions a deep-water transshipment port, an international airport, a greenfield township, and a defence and
strategic services hub. The plan has attracted significant attention from environmental scientists, constitutional
scholars, tribal rights advocates, and maritime strategists. Critics point to concerns about large-scale forest
diversion, impacts on marine and terrestrial biodiversity, and the rights of indigenous communities, while
proponents emphasise the project's strategic and economic imperatives for India.


Q13. The indigenous tribal communities of the Andaman and Nicobar Islands, including the Shompen and the
Great Andamanese, enjoy statutory protection from outsider contact and encroachment under a specific colonial-
era regulation retained in independent India. Which regulation provides this protection?
    a) The Scheduled Tribes and Other Traditional Forest Dwellers (Recognition of Forest Rights) Act, 2006
    b) The Protection of Aboriginal Tribes Regulation, 1956
    c) The Andaman and Nicobar Islands (Protection of Aboriginal Tribes) Act, 1972
    d) The Particularly Vulnerable Tribal Groups Welfare Act, 2008


Q14. Great Nicobar Island's strategic value is largely premised on its proximity to a critical maritime chokepoint.
The Strait of Malacca — one of the world's most trafficked sea lanes — primarily connects which two bodies of
water?
   a) The Indian Ocean (specifically the Andaman Sea) and the South China Sea
   b) The Bay of Bengal and the Java Sea
   c) The Arabian Sea and the Banda Sea
   d) The Laccadive Sea and the Celebes Sea

Q15. The Great Nicobar Island Holistic Development Project received its Forest and Environmental Clearance from
the Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change (MoEFCC) in which year, triggering widespread public
debate?
    a) 2020
    b) 2022
    c) 2024
    d) 2019


Q16. The project area on Great Nicobar Island substantially overlaps with a UNESCO-recognised biosphere reserve
that is home to exceptional levels of endemism in both flora and fauna. Which reserve is this?
     a) Gulf of Mannar Biosphere Reserve
     b) Great Nicobar Biosphere Reserve
     c) Sundarbans Biosphere Reserve
     d) Agasthyamalai Biosphere Reserve


Q17. Which government entity has been designated as the primary nodal implementing agency for the Great
Nicobar Island Holistic Development Project?
   a) Andaman and Nicobar Islands Integrated Development Corporation (ANIIDCO)
   b) National Industrial Corridor Development Corporation (NICDC)
   c) NITI Aayog's Project Development and Monitoring Unit
   d) The Andaman and Nicobar Command of the Indian Armed Forces


Q18. Environmental scientists opposing the Great Nicobar Project have highlighted that the beaches of the island
serve as the single largest nesting ground in the Indian Ocean for a critically endangered marine species. Which
species is this, and what makes its case particularly significant?
    a) Olive Ridley Sea Turtle — it is listed as Vulnerable under the IUCN Red List and is the most abundant sea
    turtle species globally
    b) Leatherback Sea Turtle — it is the world's largest sea turtle, listed as Vulnerable globally but critically
    threatened in the Indian Ocean, and nests in large numbers on Great Nicobar's beaches
    c) Green Sea Turtle — it is critically endangered globally and its nesting on Great Nicobar constitutes 80% of
    India's total population
    d) Hawksbill Sea Turtle — it is critically endangered and its shells are used in traditional Nicobarese craft



Passage IV


Maritime transport is the backbone of global commerce, carrying an estimated 90% of world trade by volume. The
legal framework governing the use of the world's oceans is primarily codified in the United Nations Convention on
the Law of the Sea (UNCLOS), adopted in 1982 and in force since 1994, often described as the 'constitution of the
oceans.' It delineates maritime zones — including internal waters, territorial seas, contiguous zones, exclusive
economic zones, and the high seas — and prescribes the rights and obligations of states in each.
India, with a coastline of approximately 7,516 kilometres, a vast Exclusive Economic Zone, and a significant
merchant fleet, has consistently positioned itself as an advocate for the freedom of navigation and unimpeded
maritime commerce. In recent years, global shipping has been severely disrupted by attacks on commercial vessels

in the Red Sea corridor by Houthi militants, forcing rerouting of major trade routes. India has called for safe and
unimpeded maritime transport in various multilateral forums, underscoring that freedom of navigation is
foundational to global trade and the rules-based international order.


Q19. Under UNCLOS, the right of 'innocent passage' allows foreign ships to transit a coastal state's maritime zone
without prior authorisation, provided the passage is continuous, expeditious, and not prejudicial to the peace, good
order, or security of the coastal state. Through which specific maritime zone does this right of innocent passage
apply?
    a) The Exclusive Economic Zone (EEZ), extending up to 200 nautical miles
    b) The Contiguous Zone, extending from 12 to 24 nautical miles
    c) The Territorial Sea, extending up to 12 nautical miles from the baseline
    d) The High Seas, beyond any national jurisdiction


Q20. The philosophical underpinning of the modern freedom of the high seas doctrine can be traced to the seminal
work 'Mare Liberum' (The Free Sea), published in 1609. Who authored this work, and against which colonial
power's claims over exclusive sea routes was it principally directed?
   a) Hugo Grotius, directed against Portuguese claims of exclusive dominion over the Indian Ocean trade routes
   b) Emerich de Vattel, directed against British claims of sovereignty over the English Channel
   c) Francisco de Vitoria, directed against Spanish monopoly claims over Pacific Ocean routes
   d) Samuel Pufendorf, directed against Dutch claims of exclusive fishing rights in the North Sea


Q21. Houthi militant attacks on international commercial shipping in the Red Sea since late 2023 have primarily
targeted vessels transiting through which strategic chokepoint, disrupting trade between Asia, Europe, and East
Africa?
    a) The Strait of Hormuz, between Iran and the Arabian Peninsula
    b) The Bab-el-Mandeb Strait, between Yemen and the Horn of Africa, connecting the Red Sea to the Gulf of
    Aden
    c) The Suez Canal proper, within Egyptian sovereign territory
    d) The Strait of Malacca, between Malaysia and Indonesia


Q22. India, while supporting freedom of navigation and condemning attacks on commercial shipping, declined to
formally join the US-led naval coalition assembled to counter Houthi threats in the Red Sea. Instead, India
independently deployed Indian Navy warships for escort and deterrence missions. By what name was this US-led
maritime coalition operation known?
    a) Operation Inherent Resolve
    b) Operation Prosperity Guardian
    c) Operation Unified Protector
    d) Operation Active Endeavour


Q23. India has been engaged in counter-piracy operations in the Gulf of Aden under the authority of a UN Security
Council Resolution that permitted states to enter Somali territorial waters to repress acts of piracy and armed
robbery. Which UNSC Resolution, first provided this authorisation?
    a) UNSC Resolution 1267 (1999)
    b) UNSC Resolution 1816 (2008)
    c) UNSC Resolution 2231 (2015)

d) UNSC Resolution 1540 (2004)


Q24. The International Maritime Organization (IMO), which sets global standards for the safety, security, and
environmental performance of international shipping, is a specialised agency of the United Nations. Which of the
following correctly identifies its headquarters and its current Secretary-General (as of 2024)?
    a) Geneva, Switzerland; Kitack Lim of South Korea
    b) London, United Kingdom; Arsenio Dominguez of Panama
    c) New York, United States; Efthimios Mitropoulos of Greece
    d) The Hague, Netherlands; Guy Platten of the United Kingdom



Passage V


Bats, constituting the order Chiroptera, are the only mammals capable of true sustained flight and represent
approximately one-fifth of all classified mammal species worldwide — the second largest mammalian order after
rodents. Their ecological services are extraordinarily diverse: they act as pollinators for hundreds of plant species
(including economically significant ones such as agave and durian), as seed dispersers critical to forest regeneration,
and as insect predators that provide natural pest control conservatively valued at billions of dollars annually to
global agriculture.
In a landmark scientific development, the first-ever comprehensive global assessment of bat conservation status
was published, covering thousands of bat species across every biogeographic region. The assessment raised
significant alarms: it identified numerous species as threatened under IUCN Red List criteria, highlighted endemic
species concentrated in island ecosystems as particularly at risk, and flagged large portions of tropical diversity as
'data deficient' — representing what researchers termed 'data dark spots.' These gaps, concentrated in species-rich
tropical regions, severely hamper the ability of conservation managers to prioritise resources and develop effective
protection strategies.


Q25. The IUCN Red List employs quantitative criteria to classify species by their risk of extinction. A bat species
population with fewer than 250 mature individuals and a continuing decline in the number of mature individuals
would be assigned to which Red List category?
   a) Vulnerable
   b) Endangered
   c) Critically Endangered
   d) Near Threatened


Q26. The wing membrane of bats, which is stretched between elongated finger bones, the body, the hind limbs,
and often the tail, enabling true powered flight, is known by which anatomical term?
    a) Patagium (plural: patagia)
    b) Remex (plural: remiges)
    c) Alula
    d) Calcar

Q27. The first-ever global bat conservation status assessment was conducted under the auspices of which body,
which is the primary IUCN expert group responsible for bat taxonomy, ecology, and conservation globally?
   a) IUCN SSC Chiroptera Specialist Group
   b) World Wildlife Fund Global Bat Programme
   c) BatLife International Conservation Alliance
   d) The Global Chiroptera Conservation Partnership under UNEP


Q28. The bat conservation assessment specifically coined the term 'data dark spots' to describe a systemic problem
in the science. What does this term refer to in the context of the assessment?
     a) Cave systems rendered inaccessible to researchers due to white-nose syndrome fungal contamination
     b) Geographic regions, predominantly in the tropics and island ecosystems, where insufficient scientific data
     exists on bat species diversity, population status, and ecological requirements to assign a reliable Red List
     category
     c) Areas where artificial light pollution disrupts bat foraging and echolocation, creating invisible ecological
     traps
     d) Species for which only skeletal remains exist, preventing assessment of contemporary population trends


Q29. India has faced recurrent outbreaks of a bat-borne zoonotic paramyxovirus, primarily in the state of Kerala,
that causes acute encephalitis and respiratory illness in humans with a case fatality rate of 40–75%. Which virus is
this, and which bat genus serves as its primary natural reservoir?
     a) Hendra virus; Rhinolophus (horseshoe bats)
     b) Nipah virus; Pteropus (fruit bats / flying foxes)
     c) Marburg virus; Rousettus (Egyptian fruit bats)
     d) SARS-CoV-2; Rhinolophus affinis (Chinese horseshoe bat)


Q30. The global bat conservation assessment flagged which geographic region as having the most significant 'data
dark spots,' combining high species richness with the lowest density of scientific surveys and the highest proportion
of Data Deficient species?
    a) North America and the Arctic tundra
    b) Sub-Saharan Africa and Southeast Asian archipelagos
    c) High-altitude Himalayan zones and the Tibetan Plateau
    d) The Caribbean islands and the southern cone of South America



Passage VI


The 'rules-based international order' refers to the architecture of shared norms, institutions, and legal frameworks
constructed primarily in the aftermath of World War II, centred on the United Nations Charter, the Universal
Declaration of Human Rights, the principles of state sovereignty and non-intervention, and the multilateral dispute
resolution mechanisms of bodies such as the World Trade Organization and the International Court of Justice. In
recent years, this order has been subjected to mounting stress from unilateral military actions, the weaponisation of
economic interdependence, and challenges to multilateral institutions.
India, under Prime Minister Narendra Modi, has consistently articulated a nuanced position on the rules-based order:
endorsing multilateralism, the UN Charter's principles of sovereignty and territorial integrity, and peaceful

resolution of disputes, while simultaneously asserting its strategic autonomy and declining to align formally with
any bloc. In a series of high-level bilateral and multilateral meetings, including with world leaders from the Global
South and key partners, India has reiterated that lasting and sustainable peace cannot be achieved through military
dominance or economic coercion, but only through adherence to international law, inclusive governance reform,
and dialogue.


Q31. The International Court of Justice (ICJ), the principal judicial organ of the United Nations, exercises
jurisdiction over inter-state disputes. Which of the following most accurately describes the basis of the ICJ's
contentious jurisdiction?
     a) Compulsory and automatic jurisdiction over all disputes between UN member states by virtue of UN
     membership.
     b) Consensual jurisdiction, arising from special agreement (compromis), treaty clauses conferring jurisdiction,
     or optional clause declarations under Article 36(2) of the ICJ Statute accepting compulsory jurisdiction
     reciprocally.
     c) Jurisdiction limited to disputes voluntarily submitted by P5 members of the UN Security Council.
     d) Advisory jurisdiction only; the ICJ cannot issue binding judgments in any contentious case.


Q32. The Preamble to the Charter of the United Nations opens with 'We the Peoples of the United Nations.' Which
of the following best captures the primary purposes articulated in the Preamble of the UN Charter?
     a) To establish a world government with supreme legislative authority over member states and ensure universal
     free trade.
     b) To save succeeding generations from the scourge of war, reaffirm faith in fundamental human rights and the
     equal rights of nations, and promote social progress and better standards of life.
     c) To guarantee collective security exclusively through military alliances and sanctions against aggressor states.
     d) To codify international law and create a binding global constitution enforceable through the ICJ.


Q33. India's position on the Russia-Ukraine conflict has been marked by strategic abstention in multiple UN General
Assembly resolutions calling for Russian withdrawal. Which of the following most precisely characterises India's
publicly stated diplomatic rationale?
   a) India explicitly endorses Russia's position that the conflict is a domestic security matter.
   b) India, invoking its long-standing tradition of strategic autonomy, has called for dialogue and diplomacy,
   declined to sanction Russia, continued to purchase discounted Russian crude oil, and voted against resolutions
   that it viewed as prejudging the outcome of negotiations rather than promoting peace.
   c) India has supported NATO's position and called for an immediate international arms embargo on Russia.
   d) India endorsed the ICC's arrest warrant against President Putin and called for his prosecution before the
   International Criminal Court.


Q34. India is a member of the G4 group of nations, all of which aspire to permanent membership in a reformed UN
Security Council. As part of its push for a rules-based and more representative global order, India has also called
for reform of which other key multilateral institution's dispute settlement mechanism, which has been effectively
paralysed since 2019?
     a) The International Monetary Fund's quota and governance structure
     b) The World Trade Organization's Appellate Body, which has been non-functional since December 2019 due
     to the United States blocking new appointments
     c) The International Court of Justice's judge selection process
     d) The UN Human Rights Council's membership criteria

Q35. India's invocation of a 'rules-based maritime order' in the context of the South China Sea dispute is
fundamentally premised on adherence to which instrument, which China has refused to accept as the basis for
resolving its maritime claims?
    a) The 1958 Geneva Convention on the Territorial Sea and the Contiguous Zone
    b) UNCLOS and the 2016 Award by the Arbitral Tribunal constituted under Annex VII of UNCLOS in the
    Philippines v. China case, which found China's expansive 'nine-dash line' claims inconsistent with UNCLOS
    c) The ASEAN Maritime Security Framework of 2017
    d) The Colombo Process Declaration on Freedom of Navigation, 2023


Q36. India has been actively advocating for reform of the UN Security Council veto system. Which of the following
most accurately reflects India's stated position on the veto power in recent multilateral negotiations on UNSC
reform?
    a) India calls for the complete and immediate abolition of the veto power for all permanent members.
    b) India supports extending the veto power as currently constituted to all new permanent members, including
    India itself.
    c) India has supported restricting the use of the veto — particularly in situations involving mass atrocities and
    genocide — while seeking a permanent seat without initially demanding veto parity, and has backed the
    Liechtenstein-led 'Veto Initiative' requiring the UNGA to convene when a veto is cast.
    d) India has proposed replacing the individual veto with a collective veto system requiring concurrence of at
    least three P5 members for a veto to be valid.



Passage VII


India's civil nuclear energy sector has since independence been governed by a strict state-monopoly framework.
The Atomic Energy Act of 1962, enacted under the stewardship of the Department of Atomic Energy (DAE) —
which operates under the direct charge of the Prime Minister — vests exclusive authority over nuclear power
generation in government-owned entities. The Nuclear Power Corporation of India Limited (NPCIL) and its
subsidiary Bharatiya Nabhikiya Vidyut Nigam Limited (BHAVINI), responsible for fast breeder reactor
development, are the sole entities currently authorised to operate nuclear power plants in India.
In a significant policy shift, India's atomic energy establishment has cleared the framework for Foreign Direct
Investment (FDI) in the nuclear power sector, with a public consultation process announced as the next step before
final notification. This development is part of India's broader ambition to substantially scale up its nuclear installed
capacity as part of its clean energy transition. A key impediment to international investment in India's nuclear sector
has historically been the Civil Liability for Nuclear Damage Act of 2010, whose supplier liability provisions have
deterred major foreign nuclear equipment manufacturers.


Q37. India's nuclear programme was conceived and launched under the visionary leadership of a pioneering
physicist who served as the first Chairman of the Atomic Energy Commission of India, established in 1948. Who
was this individual, and by what informal title has he come to be remembered in the history of Indian science?
   a) Dr. Vikram Sarabhai; father of India's space programme
   b) Dr. Homi J. Bhabha; father of India's nuclear programme
   c) Dr. Raja Ramanna; the architect of Pokhran-I

d) Dr. A.P.J. Abdul Kalam; the missile man of India


Q38. India's officially declared nuclear doctrine, as articulated in the Cabinet Committee on Security's press
statement of January 2003, includes a 'No First Use' (NFU) policy. However, the doctrine identifies one specific
exception under which India reserves the right to respond with nuclear weapons even if the adversary has not used
nuclear weapons first. What is this exception?
     a) In the event of a conventional military attack that threatens the territorial integrity of India
     b) In the event of a major attack against India or Indian forces anywhere with biological or chemical weapons
     c) In the event of a nuclear attack on any ally state that has a mutual defence treaty with India
     d) There is no exception — India's NFU is unconditional and absolute under all circumstances


Q39. Section 17(b) of the Civil Liability for Nuclear Damage Act (CLND Act), 2010 has been the single most
contentious provision for foreign nuclear suppliers seeking to do business in India. What right does Section 17(b)
specifically grant?
    a) It grants the nuclear operator (NPCIL) the right of recourse against the supplier of equipment or material if
    the nuclear incident is caused by a patent or latent defect in the supplied equipment, or the supplier has provided
    sub-standard services.
    b) It grants the Central Government the right to nationalise foreign-owned nuclear assets in the event of a
    nuclear emergency.
    c) It grants victims of a nuclear accident the right to directly sue the foreign supplier before an international
    arbitral tribunal.
    d) It exempts the operator from any liability if the accident is attributable to a design defect in the reactor
    supplied by a foreign vendor.


Q40. India has articulated an ambitious nuclear power expansion target as part of its Viksit Bharat 2047 energy
vision. What is the target for nuclear installed capacity that India aims to achieve by the centenary of Independence?
    a) 20 GW
    b) 63 GW
    c) 100 GW
    d) 500 GW


Q41. The proposed FDI policy for the nuclear power sector, if implemented, would require an amendment to the
primary legislation that currently restricts nuclear power generation exclusively to government entities. Which is
this legislation?
     a) The Nuclear Power Corporation of India Limited Act, 1987, which established NPCIL as a corporate entity
     b) The Atomic Energy Act, 1962, which vests exclusive rights to produce, develop, use, and dispose of atomic
     energy in the Central Government
     c) The Electricity Act, 2003, which governs the overall electricity sector including generation licensing
     d) The Foreign Exchange Management Act (FEMA), 1999, which regulates all inbound foreign investment


Q42. Dr. Homi J. Bhabha's three-stage nuclear power programme, which has shaped India's nuclear strategy for
decades, envisages utilising India's vast thorium reserves in the third and final stage. What fissile material is
produced and used in the third stage, and from what is it bred?
    a) Plutonium-239, bred from Uranium-238 in fast breeder reactors
    b) Uranium-235, enriched from natural uranium mined domestically

c) Uranium-233, bred from Thorium-232 in reactors fuelled by the plutonium generated in stage two
    d) Deuterium and Tritium, sourced from heavy water to power fusion reactors in the final stage



Passage VIII


The Overseas Citizen of India (OCI) card is an immigration status that confers upon persons of Indian origin a
multi-purpose, multi-entry, lifelong visa to visit India and near-parity with Non-Resident Indians (NRIs) in most
economic, financial, and educational activities. Introduced by the Citizenship (Amendment) Act, 2005, the OCI
scheme replaced and subsequently subsumed the earlier Person of Indian Origin (PIO) card in 2015. OCI holders
are not, however, citizens of India — they do not have the right to vote, hold constitutional offices, or acquire
agricultural or plantation land.
India recently announced an extension of OCI card eligibility for persons of Indian origin in Sri Lanka up to the
sixth generation. This development carries deep historical resonance: a substantial proportion of the Indian-origin
community in Sri Lanka are descendants of Tamil workers brought to the island by British colonial authorities to
labour in the highland tea and rubber plantations. This community's citizenship status became a protracted
diplomatic and humanitarian issue following Sri Lanka's independence, resulting in a series of bilateral agreements
between the two nations. India's move is seen as an act of diaspora outreach as well as a signal of the deepening of
bilateral ties between the two South Asian neighbours.

       The Jan Vishwas (Amendment to Provisions) Bill, 2026

Parliament recently passed a reform-oriented Bill to revise numerous provisions across several Central
laws. The measure continues an earlier effort to simplify the legal framework and promote ease of doing
business by reducing the use of criminal sanctions for minor regulatory violations.
The Bill introduces a broad shift in approach by replacing criminal punishment in many cases with civil
penalties, warnings, or settlement mechanisms. Instead of treating every non-compliance as a criminal
offence requiring police action and court proceedings, the law seeks to reserve criminal liability for more
serious harms.
It also removes outdated provisions, modifies excessive punishments, and allows certain disputes to be
resolved through compounding. This reflects an attempt to create a more proportionate legal system where
enforcement is based on the seriousness of the violation.
The reform raises larger questions about the role of the state in regulating conduct. It highlights the
distinction between punitive criminal law and administrative regulation, while also reflecting the need for
laws to evolve with changing economic and social realities.

Women’s Quota Reservation Bill
The Union government is considering a set of legislative measures aimed at accelerating the
implementation of women’s reservation in legislative bodies. These proposals seek to overcome

procedural delays by relying on previously available population data instead of waiting for a fresh
nationwide exercise.
A key component of this plan involves revisiting the process of redrawing electoral boundaries and
adjusting the number of seats in representative institutions. This process is closely tied to population
distribution, as representation is intended to reflect demographic realities. Any change in the number of
seats or their boundaries would therefore have significant implications for political representation across
regions.
At the same time, such reforms raise broader questions about fairness and balance in representation.
Differences in population growth rates across states may influence how political power is distributed,
leading to debates about whether representation should be based solely on population or also consider
other factors such as governance performance and economic contribution.
The proposal highlights the complex relationship between constitutional provisions, democratic
representation, and social justice objectives. It underscores the challenges involved in designing reforms
that are both equitable and practically implementable within a diverse federal framework.
